title: CS6460 Module 5 · Scene quiz
note: 33 Know scenes, 7 practice-sample items, 90 practice-bank items. Session draws 5. Explains are layman + why each wrong dies.

items.stem: On a practice run a learner scores 18. Classical Test Theory treats that 18 how?

choices.text: As Observed Score = True Score + Error — the number is never pure truth.
As True Score = Observed Score + Error, rearranging the same idea incorrectly.
As Observed Score = Criterion Score + Norm Score.
As Observed Score = True Score + Percentile Rank.

items.explain: The score you see is true ability plus mess — Observed = True + Error. Flipping True and Observed is the wrong equation. Criterion/norm and percentile are other ideas, not that central equation.

items.stem: A dashboard swings wildly from day to day for the same learner with no real change. Why does that block validity claims?

choices.text: A measurement dominated by random error cannot be a trustworthy signal of any construct — reliability ceilings validity.
High reliability automatically proves the tool is valid for its purpose.
Validity sets the maximum reliability a score can ever reach.
Fairness to groups is unrelated to reliability.

items.explain: If the number is mostly noise, it cannot honestly point at the skill you care about. Reliable still is not automatically valid. Validity does not cap reliability that way. Fairness can still interact with reliability.

items.stem: A certification exam has Cronbach alpha 0.95 across cohorts. Marketing wants to call it 'validated job readiness.' Strongest measurement objection?

choices.text: Consistency does not say what is being measured — highly reliable scores can still be invalid for that claim.
Internal consistency cannot be computed once more than one cohort exists.
The claim holds if the exam is criterion-referenced instead of norm-referenced.
The claim holds once standard error falls below one scale point.

items.explain: A steady score can still measure the wrong thing. Multi-cohort consistency is computable. Criterion vs norm referencing and tiny standard error do not by themselves prove job-readiness validity.

items.stem: A scale weighs you at 182.0 every morning for a week — same number each day — but the true weight is 168 because it was never calibrated. What does that illustrate?

choices.text: High consistency (reliability) with the wrong target (invalid for true weight).
Low reliability but high validity.
That reliability and validity are the same word.
That calibration is irrelevant once scores stop bouncing.

items.explain: Same wrong number every day is reliable and still wrong. That is not low reliability. Reliability and validity are not synonyms. Calibration is exactly why the steady wrong reading fails.

items.stem: Asked to compare two sorting algorithms, a student writes a joke about laundry 'sorting' and never addresses runtime. Which SOLO stage fits?

choices.text: Prestructural — misses the point with irrelevant or tautological engagement.
Unistructural — one relevant element, narrowly connected.
Multistructural — several relevant elements, unintegrated.
Extended abstract — generalizes to a new domain.

items.explain: Prestructural = misses the point. One relevant bit would be unistructural. Several unconnected relevant bits would be multistructural. Extended abstract goes up a level of abstraction on purpose.

items.stem: The lesson names Bloom's hierarchy problem and type problem. What is the type problem?

choices.text: Bloom handles how demanding a task is better than what kind of learning it represents.
Bloom cannot be used on open-ended work at all.
Bloom ignores motor and attitude domains entirely by definition.
Bloom handles kind of learning well but says nothing about demand.

items.explain: The type problem is weak on *kind* of learning while demand/hierarchy is handled better. Open-ended work is not banned. Motor/attitude domains are a different issue. The last option flips type vs demand.

items.stem: A final reuses the identical three troubleshooting tickets from last month's homework, then claims 'debugging mastery.' Strongest objection?

choices.text: Reused instances cannot separate intellectual skill from memory of those specific tickets.
Reuse is always best because retrieval practice prefers identical items forever.
The final should open with an advance organizer naming the homework.
Switching to a SOLO rubric alone fixes the reuse problem.

items.explain: Same tickets can be memorized as stories, not as transferable debugging skill. Identical forever is not required for retrieval practice. An advance organizer or SOLO rubric does not fix the confound.

items.stem: A course adds daily auto-graded clicker items because they are cheap. Over a term, discussions and design critiques shrink. What danger does the lesson flag?

choices.text: Frequent cheap auto-gradable checks can quietly narrow the course toward whatever the software can grade.
They always raise stakes until learners hide confusion.
They overload working memory by definition.
They make every score stop separating learners.

items.explain: What the machine can score starts to become the whole course. Stakes, working memory, and separation can fail in other designs — they are not the narrowing danger named here.

items.stem: Why does the lesson stress that the Roediger and Karpicke testing advantage showed on a delayed test?

choices.text: Durable retention, not immediate performance, is the measure that matters.
Immediate tests are unreliable whenever a passage is read twice.
A week lets spacing replace the testing effect entirely.
Learners cannot self-judge until about a week passes.

items.explain: They care about what sticks later, not how it looks right after study. Double reading does not make immediate tests meaningless. Spacing does not erase the testing effect. Self-judgment timing is a different claim.

items.stem: A game studio wants 'stealth assessment' of engineering reasoning from play logs alone. What should they settle first under evidence-centered design?

choices.text: Which competencies they intend to measure, before deciding what counts as evidence.
Which events are cheapest to log, then invent meanings later.
Which levels feel hardest, for curve calibration first.
Which playtesters match the marketing persona.

items.explain: Decide what skill you mean to measure first, then decide which logged actions would count as proof of that skill. Cheap logs invent meaning after the fact. Hardest levels calibrate difficulty, not the construct. Playtester personas are recruiting, not the measurement model.

items.stem: In evidence-centered design, what is the competency model versus the evidence model?

choices.text: Competency model = what you intend to measure; evidence model = which observable actions count as proof.
Competency model = the LMS gradebook columns; evidence model = the curve.
Competency model = cheapest logs; evidence model = marketing claims.
They are two names for the same checklist of quiz items.

items.explain: Competencies are the targets; evidence is what you will accept as signs of those targets. Gradebook columns, curves, cheap logs, and marketing are not those two models. They are not the same checklist under two labels.

items.stem: According to the grading philosophies lesson, what four jobs is a grade asked to do?

choices.text: Communicate, sort, motivate, and give feedback.
Diagnose, sort, motivate, and remediate.
Communicate, calibrate, rank, and certify competence.
Certify, motivate, diagnose, and archive.

items.explain: Course voice: communicate, sort, motivate, feedback. The other lists swap in diagnose/remediate/calibrate/archive jobs the lesson is not using as the four.

items.stem: What most distinguishes contract grading from standards-based and specifications grading?

choices.text: It changes who decides the grade and what the grade is based on in the first place.
It alone uses written descriptions of acceptable quality.
It alone permits reassessment.
It alone reports each objective separately.

items.explain: Contract grading shifts who decides and on what basis. Written quality bars, reassessment, and separate objectives show up in the sibling systems too.

items.stem: Students chase safe projects that score well and ignore written critique beyond the letter at the top. Faculty conclude the mark itself is the problem. Which philosophy follows?

choices.text: Ungrading — replace the reported number with feedback and a closing conversation.
Standards-based grading — report each objective as a separate mastery mark.
Specifications grading — judge each piece against a written bar.
Contract grading — tie the grade to labor agreed in advance.

items.explain: If the letter/number is distorting behavior, ungrading removes that symbol. The other philosophies still center a reported mark structure.

items.stem: Match the philosophy to the move: (1) remove the score symbol, (2) agree labor/engagement up front, (3) judge each piece against a written quality bar.

choices.text: 1 ungrading, 2 contract grading, 3 specifications grading.
1 specifications, 2 ungrading, 3 contract.
1 contract, 2 specifications, 3 ungrading.
1 standards-based, 2 ungrading, 3 contract.

items.explain: Ungrading drops the mark. Contract shifts the bargain of who decides. Specifications uses an explicit quality bar per piece. The other matchings scramble those.

items.stem: A studio mentor can spot strong critique in seconds but struggles to write the rule for new TAs. Sadler would call that mentor's sense what?

choices.text: Guild knowledge — the expert's often-tacit sense of what good work looks like.
The published rubric criteria handed out before work begins.
The shared vocabulary of a discipline's citation rules alone.
Only procedures a newcomer masters by peripheral participation.

items.explain: Guild knowledge is the hard-to-say expert feel for quality. A printed rubric is explicit. Citation vocabulary alone is narrower. Peripheral participation is a learning path, not Sadler's name for that tacit feel.

items.stem: Carefully written comments keep bouncing. What does the lesson say is often why?

choices.text: Feedback presumes a shared standard of quality that teacher and student do not actually share.
Comments are too impersonal in register.
The LMS displays poorly on phones.
Comments were written before other papers were read.

items.explain: If teacher and student do not share what 'good' means, comments have nowhere to stick. Tone, phone layout, and grading order are lesser explanations here.

items.stem: Peer reviewers describe likes and changes but never see what the assignment was aiming at; authors call reviews arbitrary. Best fix from the lesson?

choices.text: Show reviewers the goal the work is aiming at before they write.
Let reviewers read each other before submitting their own.
Require a compliment before any critique.
Impose a fixed word count for depth.

items.explain: Without the aim, reviews cannot share a standard. Reading peers, forced compliments, or word counts do not supply the missing target.

items.stem: Which definition matches an analytic rubric?

choices.text: It breaks the work into separate criteria and scores each independently.
It compares every paper to one benchmark exemplar only.
It waits until the whole stack is read before any score.
It scores only against the range the cohort actually produced.

items.explain: Analytic = separate criteria, separate scores. One exemplar, wait-for-whole-stack, and cohort-range scoring are other rubric/grading moves.

items.stem: Rubric A awards points for naming each of three causes. Rubric B awards a pool for naming and describing causes without listing how many. Why can A assess a different construct?

choices.text: Telling students that three are wanted removes the need to recognize scope — different from recognizing and elaborating.
A is faster to grade, so it must measure the same thing.
A uses fewer total points, so incompleteness costs less.
A names the causes outright, so recall disappears entirely.

items.explain: Showing 'three' changes the mental work required. Speed and point totals do not prove same construct. The stem does not say A names the causes for the student.

items.stem: A chair wants every course from survey to seminar to publish a full grading rubric with the syllabus. How should the lesson's argument be applied?

choices.text: Reject the blanket rule; set grain and visibility course by course according to the construct assessed.
Adopt it always — hidden criteria are always unfair.
Adopt the opposite blanket ban on showing any rubric early.
Adopt it only when multiple graders share a stack.

items.explain: Whether to show a fine-grained rubric depends on what you are measuring in that course. Always-show and never-show blankets both ignore construct. Multi-grader logistics alone is not the rule.

items.stem: A team wants one overall quality judgment per essay, not separate scores for thesis, evidence, and mechanics. What are they rejecting?

choices.text: An analytic rubric's separate criteria scores — they want a holistic overall judgment instead.
Evidence-centered design entirely.
Any feedback to students.
Contract grading's labor bargain.

items.explain: One overall mark is holistic; split criteria are analytic. That choice is not rejecting ECD, feedback, or contract grading as such.

items.stem: Why does averaging many peer raters often fail to remove error?

choices.text: Peer-rater errors are often not independent of each other.
Averaging needs a dozen raters before any effect begins.
Peers always drift to the scale midpoint.
Each extra rater adds more noise than they remove by definition.

items.explain: If everyone shares the same bias, the average keeps the bias. You do not need a magic dozen. Midpoint drift is one failure mode, not the general reason. Extra raters are not automatic net noise.

items.stem: What distinguishes the reliability question from the fairness question in peer assessment?

choices.text: Reliability asks whether peer grades are consistent; fairness asks whether they are consistent for reasons that have nothing to do with the work.
Reliability asks accuracy; fairness asks whether students liked the process.
Reliability asks stability over years; fairness asks rubric coverage.
Reliability asks defensibility; fairness asks equal review workload.

items.explain: Reliability = do the marks agree. Fairness = do they agree for the wrong reasons (bias unrelated to the work). Liking the process, year-scale stability, and equal workload are different questions.

items.stem: Staff write thin, slow feedback while unread peer reviews already exist on each submission. Which redesign matches the lesson?

choices.text: Have graders evaluate each submission alongside the peer reviews it already received.
Let raw peer marks stand as the final grade.
Estimate ungraded papers from peer marks after sampling.
Make staff write feedback before peers review so peers can copy tone.

items.explain: Staff become meta-reviewers: judge the work in light of the peer reviews. Raw peer marks as final, estimating the rest from peers, or staff-first modeling are not that design — and raw peer finals are warned against.

items.stem: Peer scores on posters are almost identical across raters because everyone docks points for accent, not for poster quality. What passes and what fails?

choices.text: Reliability can look fine (they agree) while fairness fails (they agree for the wrong reason).
Fairness passes because agreement is high.
Reliability fails because scores match.
Both pass whenever scores match.

items.explain: Agreement from a shared irrelevant bias is reliable and unfair. High agreement is not fairness. Matching scores are exactly what reliability likes.

items.stem: What is undue influence in researching learners, as the lesson defines it?

choices.text: The subtler pressure of not wanting to disappoint the person who controls your academic fate.
An interface nudge the learner never notices.
A researcher reading ambiguous results in their favor.
Only the explicit threat of an academic penalty for declining.

items.explain: Undue influence is the quieter pull from the person who grades you. Dark-pattern nudges, motivated reading of results, and only blunt threats are different problems — the lesson separates undue influence from explicit coercion.

items.stem: Why is privacy in research harder than a single collection moment?

choices.text: Data often persists, gets shared, and gets re-analyzed for years in ways nobody foresaw.
Students can never object because instruments are invisible.
Aggregation always strips detail so return is impossible.
A legal exception always overrides student preferences.

items.explain: The hard part is long life and surprise reuse of the data. Invisible instruments, aggregation, and legal overrides are not the main lesson point.

items.stem: Consent covered a hint-system study. Years later another team wants that archive to train dropout prediction. Stewardship says?

choices.text: Reuse needs revisiting — one consent does not license any use forever.
Reuse is fine because no new collection occurs.
Reuse is fine after a second de-identification pass alone.
Reuse is barred because all research data must be destroyed at study end.

items.explain: New purpose needs a fresh look at consent. 'No new collection,' a second de-ID pass, or mandatory destroy-all are not the stewardship rule named.

items.stem: Syllabus says 'you may decline the study with no grade penalty,' but students still enroll because they do not want to disappoint the professor who grades them. Which problem is that?

choices.text: Undue influence — subtler pressure from the grader relationship, even without an explicit threat.
Only explicit coercion, because the syllabus already promised no penalty.
Only a validity threat to Classical Test Theory.
Only a curb-cut accessibility failure.

items.explain: No written penalty can still leave grader-power pressure — undue influence. That is not 'only coercion solved by syllabus text,' not Classical Test Theory, and not curb cuts.

items.stem: What distinguishes a biased assessment deployed at scale from one used once?

choices.text: It harms an entire population in the same direction, all at once.
It becomes merely a compliance issue, not an ethical one.
It becomes easier to ignore because errors average out.
It harms a smaller share of learners by definition.

items.explain: Scale means the same skew hits many people together. It stays ethical, does not magically average away, and does not shrink the harmed share by definition.

items.stem: Why do fairness obligations intensify with scale, especially in educational technology?

choices.text: A tool that reaches many learners visits the same bias on all of them at once.
Only regulators care about classroom assessments.
Larger populations need a separate norm table per subgroup first.
Bias is only real once a sample is statistically large.

items.explain: Wide reach multiplies the same harm. Regulation, norm tables, and statistical detectability are not the intensifier named.

items.stem: A quiz platform logs keystroke timing and mouse paths 'in case analytics wants them later.' Nothing affects scores; no IRB study is running. Lesson conclusion?

choices.text: Learners are owed the privacy interest anyway — capture only what the assessment requires.
Obligations begin only if findings are published later.
Terms of service already satisfy the obligation.
Only the licensing institution holds any duty.

items.explain: No live study and no score use still do not excuse vacuuming traces 'for someday.' Publication later, ToS checkboxes, and 'blame the school' do not clear the product team.

items.stem: According to the Measurement Fundamentals lesson's on-screen text, which equation expresses the central relationship in Classical Test Theory?

choices.text: Observed Score = True Score + Error.
Observed Score = True Score + Percentile Rank.
True Score = Observed Score + Error.
Observed Score = Criterion Score + Norm Score.

items.explain: Observed = True + Error. Percentile and criterion/norm mixes are other ideas. Flipping True and Observed is the wrong equation.

items.stem: What does the Measurement Fundamentals lesson mean when it says that reliability sets a ceiling on validity?

choices.text: A measurement dominated by random error cannot be a trustworthy signal of any construct.
A measurement that is highly reliable has thereby been shown to be valid for its purpose.
A measurement's validity limits how reliable its scores are able to become in practice.
A measurement can be no fairer to a group than its reliability for that group allows.

items.explain: Noise blocks a trustworthy signal of the thing you care about. High reliability does not prove validity. Validity does not cap reliability that way. Fairness is a related but different sentence.

items.stem: A studio is building a bridge-construction game and wants to measure engineering reasoning from play alone, with no quizzes anywhere in the product. Following evidence-centered design, what should the team settle first?

choices.text: Which competencies they intend to measure, before deciding what counts as evidence.
Which in-game actions the engine can log most cheaply, before deciding what they mean.
Which levels are the hardest, so that the difficulty curve can be calibrated before launch.
Which players to recruit for playtesting, so that the sample matches the target audience.

items.explain: Decide what skill you mean to measure first, then decide which logged actions would count as proof. Cheap logs invent meaning afterward. Hard levels calibrate difficulty. Playtester personas are recruiting.

items.stem: According to the Feedback Frameworks lesson, what did Sadler call guild knowledge?

choices.text: The expert's often-tacit, hard-to-articulate sense of what good work looks like.
The list of criteria published in a rubric before learners begin an assignment.
The body of procedures a newcomer masters, learned by working at the edge.
The shared vocabulary a discipline uses to describe its standards of evidence.

items.explain: Guild knowledge is the expert's hard-to-say feel for quality. Rubrics are explicit. Edge procedures and shared vocabulary are neighboring ideas, not Sadler's name for that tacit sense.

items.stem: What distinguishes the reliability question from the fairness question in peer assessment?

choices.text: Reliability asks whether peer grades are consistent, while fairness asks whether they are consistent for reasons that have nothing to do with the work.
Reliability asks whether peer grades are accurate, while fairness asks whether students found the process transparent.
Reliability asks whether peer grades are stable over time, while fairness asks whether the rubric covered every objective.
Reliability asks whether peer grades are defensible, while fairness asks whether everyone did an equal share of reviewing.

items.explain: Reliability = do they agree. Fairness = do they agree for irrelevant reasons. Transparency liking, long-term stability, rubric coverage, and equal workload are different tests.

items.stem: A large online course has eight graders who each write feedback from scratch on three hundred submissions. Feedback is thin and slow. Peer review already happens before grading, and those reviews currently go unread by staff. Which redesign best matches the Peer Assessment lesson?

choices.text: Have graders evaluate each submission alongside the peer reviews it received.
Have graders mark a random sample and estimate the rest from the peer marks.
Have graders read only the peer reviews and let the peer marks stand as the final grade.
Have graders write their feedback before peers review, so peers have a model to imitate.

items.explain: Graders judge the work with the peer reviews in view — meta-review. Estimating from peers, crowning raw peer marks, or staff-first modeling are not that redesign.

items.stem: Which of the following is the most correct definition of undue influence?

choices.text: The subtler pressure of not wanting to disappoint the person who grades you.
The pull an interface exerts on a learner's choices without the learner noticing it.
The tendency of a researcher to read ambiguous results in favor of their own hypothesis.
The explicit threat that declining to participate will carry an academic penalty.

items.explain: Undue influence is quieter grader-power pressure. Dark-pattern pull, motivated interpretation, and explicit academic threats are neighboring problems — the last is coercion, not the subtler case.

items.stem: A research team says it wants to measure “collaborative problem solving.” Before collecting any scores, the team specifies that successful learners should propose alternatives, respond to teammates' ideas, and revise a solution after disagreement. What step has the team primarily taken?

choices.text: Established test-retest reliability
Operationalized the construct
Established criterion validity
Converted the measure to a norm-referenced scale

items.explain: Operationalization means deciding before data collection which observable indicators will count as evidence of an abstract construct. Test-retest is stability over time, criterion validity ties scores to an outside outcome, and norm referencing compares people - none of them define what counts.
items.bankWhy: Operationalization means turning an abstract construct into observable, measurable indicators. “Collaborative problem solving” cannot be measured directly until the team decides what behaviors will count as evidence of it.

items.stem: An admissions exam strongly predicts students' first-year college GPA. What type of validity evidence does this most directly provide?

choices.text: Construct validity
Internal consistency
Criterion validity
Differential item functioning

items.explain: Criterion validity is evidence that scores relate to an external outcome, here later GPA. Construct validity would ask whether the intended trait is measured, internal consistency only shows items agree with each other, and DIF is about group differences on an item.
items.bankWhy: Criterion validity asks whether scores relate to some external outcome or criterion. Predicting later GPA is the classic kind of example.

items.stem: A creativity test predicts which students will win an unrelated scholarship, but researchers discover that the test mainly measures vocabulary knowledge rather than creativity. What is the strongest concern?

choices.text: The test lacks construct validity
The test lacks a reference group
The test must have low reliability
The test is necessarily criterion-referenced

items.explain: A test can predict an outside outcome and still measure the wrong thing, so construct validity is the operative question. A missing reference group, low reliability, and criterion referencing are separate issues the scenario never establishes.
items.bankWhy: Construct validity asks whether the assessment actually measures the intended underlying construct. An assessment can correlate with an outside outcome while still measuring the wrong thing.

items.stem: Two students of essentially identical ability repeatedly receive very different scores on the same assessment under nearly identical conditions. Which measurement property is most directly in question?

choices.text: Reliability
Criterion validity
Operationalization
Norm referencing

items.explain: Reliability is consistency: would comparable conditions produce approximately the same result? Criterion validity, operationalization, and norm referencing concern meaning and reference frames, not whether the same conditions reproduce the same score.
items.bankWhy: Reliability concerns consistency: under comparable circumstances, would measurement produce approximately the same result?

items.stem: An instructor reports that a new exam has a Cronbach's alpha of .96 and therefore concludes that the exam is an excellent measure of scientific reasoning. What is the best response?

choices.text: A high alpha establishes both reliability and construct validity
A high alpha indicates consistency, but does not establish that the exam measures scientific reasoning
Alpha can only be used for norm-referenced tests
An alpha above .90 means standard error is zero

items.explain: A high alpha shows the items hang together, not that they measure scientific reasoning. A swaps reliability in for validity, C invents a norm-referenced restriction, and D reads consistency as zero error.
items.bankWhy: Reliability is necessary for a useful measure but does not tell you what is being measured. A highly consistent test can consistently measure the wrong construct.

items.stem: What does the statement **“reliability places a ceiling on validity”** mean?

choices.text: Once reliability is sufficiently high, validity follows automatically
An assessment cannot meaningfully measure a construct if its scores are overwhelmed by random measurement error
Valid measures must always have higher validity coefficients than reliability coefficients
Reliability is more important than validity in high-stakes testing

items.explain: If score variation is mostly random noise the number cannot carry a trustworthy signal about the construct, so reliability constrains validity. A turns the ceiling into a guarantee, C flips the relation, and D is a priorities claim the idea never makes.
items.bankWhy: If scores vary largely because of random noise, they cannot provide a trustworthy signal about the underlying construct. High reliability is not sufficient for validity, but very poor reliability constrains it.

items.stem: A student earns a 74 on an exam. The instructor tells the student, “You know exactly 74% of the course material.” Which concept most directly challenges that interpretation?

choices.text: Bloom's taxonomy
Standard error of measurement
Criterion referencing
Evidence-centered design

items.explain: Every observed score carries error, so 74 is a band around true ability rather than an exact percentage of material known. Bloom, criterion referencing, and evidence-centered design say nothing about one score's precision.
items.bankWhy: Any observed score contains measurement error. The student's underlying score is better understood as lying somewhere around the observed score rather than being exactly 74.

items.stem: A student is told, “You scored higher than 82% of the students in the comparison group.” What kind of interpretation is this?

choices.text: Criterion-referenced
Construct-referenced
Norm-referenced
Standards-based

items.explain: The score means something by comparison with a reference group. Criterion and standards-based readings compare against a defined standard, and construct-referenced is not one of the lesson's frames.
items.bankWhy: The meaning of the score comes from comparison with other people in a reference group.

items.stem: A certification exam reports only whether each candidate can safely perform every required laboratory procedure, regardless of how other candidates perform. Which approach best describes the interpretation?

choices.text: Norm-referenced
Criterion-referenced
Ipsative
Differential

items.explain: Each candidate is judged against a defined standard, not against other candidates. Norm-referenced would need a comparison group, ipsative compares a learner to their own past scores, and differential is not a reference frame.
items.bankWhy: The candidate is compared with a defined standard rather than with other test takers.

items.stem: A geometry exam gives lengthy, linguistically complex word problems. Students still learning English score substantially lower even after researchers match the groups on geometry ability. What is the strongest measurement concern?

choices.text: The test may be measuring geometry plus English-language proficiency
The assessment has become summative rather than formative
The exam is too criterion-referenced
The scores are necessarily unreliable

items.explain: Fairness sits inside validity: irrelevant language demands shift scores systematically, so the exam measures geometry plus English proficiency. Formative versus summative is about use, criterion referencing is a frame, and unreliability does not follow.
items.bankWhy: Fairness is part of validity. If irrelevant language demands systematically influence results, the assessment is not cleanly measuring the intended construct.

items.stem: Two groups of students have equivalent estimated mathematics ability, but one group is substantially more likely to miss one particular item. Which analysis is designed to detect this problem?

choices.text: Cronbach's alpha
Differential item functioning
Standard error of measurement
Criterion validation

items.explain: DIF detects items on which equally capable learners perform differently by group membership. Alpha is internal consistency, SEM is score error, and criterion validation links scores to an outside outcome.
items.bankWhy: DIF looks for items on which equally capable learners perform differently as a function of group membership.

items.stem: Before a difficult test, researchers ask students to identify a social identity associated with a negative stereotype about performance in the subject. Scores then fall for that group. Which phenomenon most directly describes the result?

choices.text: Criteria compliance
Stereotype threat
Testing effect
Constructive alignment

items.explain: Steele and Aronson showed that making a negatively stereotyped identity salient can suppress performance without changing underlying ability. Criteria compliance, the testing effect, and constructive alignment are different mechanisms.
items.bankWhy: Steele and Aronson's work showed that making a negatively stereotyped identity salient can suppress performance even without changing underlying ability.

items.stem: An instructor writes an extremely difficult examination composed entirely of obscure factual-recall questions. According to the lesson's use of Bloom's taxonomy, what is the strongest conclusion?

choices.text: Difficulty automatically moves the assessment into Analysis or Evaluation
The exam still primarily measures a low level of Bloom's taxonomy
Bloom's taxonomy cannot classify difficult questions
Recall questions are necessarily invalid

items.explain: Bloom classifies the cognitive operation a task demands, not how obscure or hard the content is. Difficulty does not promote recall into Analysis, Bloom can classify difficult items, and recall items are not automatically invalid.
items.bankWhy: Bloom is about the kind of cognitive operation required, not how obscure or difficult the content happens to be.

items.stem: What major change distinguishes Anderson and Krathwohl's revised Bloom taxonomy?

choices.text: It removes higher-order cognition entirely
It replaces cognitive levels with motor-skill levels
It uses action-oriented categories and adds a separate knowledge dimension
It treats all cognitive tasks as equally demanding

items.explain: The revision switches to action verbs and crosses the cognitive-process dimension with factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge. It removes nothing, adds no motor levels, and does not flatten demands.
items.bankWhy: The revision moves toward verbs and crosses the cognitive-process dimension with factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge.

items.stem: A professor objects that Bloom's hierarchy implies that lower-level tasks must always precede higher-level thinking, even though some apparently simple tasks can require substantial reasoning. Which alternative most directly addresses the **depth** of thinking required without asserting the same ladder?

choices.text: Webb's Depth of Knowledge
Cronbach's alpha
Specifications grading
SOLO Prestructural

items.explain: Webb's Depth of Knowledge describes how deep the thinking in a task goes without claiming lower levels must always come first. Alpha, specifications grading, and SOLO Prestructural measure completely different things.

items.stem: A student lists four relevant causes of an event but explains each separately and never shows how they interact. Under SOLO, which level best describes the response?

choices.text: Unistructural
Multistructural
Relational
Extended Abstract

items.explain: Several relevant elements are present but stay disconnected, which is multistructural. Unistructural has one relevant element, relational integrates them into a whole, and extended abstract goes beyond the given material.
items.bankWhy: Several relevant elements are present, but they remain disconnected.

items.stem: A learner identifies several factors, connects them into a coherent explanation, and shows how they jointly produce an outcome. Which SOLO stage best fits?

choices.text: Prestructural
Unistructural
Relational
Extended Abstract

items.explain: Relational responses integrate the components into one coherent explanation. Prestructural misses the point, unistructural has a single relevant element, and extended abstract adds transfer or generalization beyond what was given.
items.bankWhy: Relational responses integrate the components into a coherent whole.

items.stem: A learner develops a coherent explanation and then generalizes the underlying principle to a new domain that was not part of the original question. Which SOLO stage is most appropriate?

choices.text: Prestructural
Multistructural
Relational
Extended Abstract

items.explain: Extended abstract goes past integration into transfer, abstraction, or generalization. Prestructural, multistructural, and relational all stay inside the material that was handed to the learner.
items.bankWhy: Extended Abstract goes beyond integration of the given material into transfer, abstraction, or generalization.

items.stem: A programming course wants to assess whether students possess the intellectual skill of debugging unfamiliar programs. Which examination design follows most directly from Gagné's framework?

choices.text: Reuse exactly the programs students practiced
Give students novel debugging problems
Ask students to define the word debugging
Give students a survey of their attitudes toward debugging

items.explain: If the target is an intellectual skill, learners must show it on novel instances rather than replay practiced examples. Reusing the same programs, defining the term, and surveying attitudes test memory, verbal knowledge, or affect instead.
items.bankWhy: If the target is an intellectual skill, the learner should demonstrate it on novel instances rather than reproduce memory for practiced examples.

items.stem: Which pairing best matches the role assigned to each taxonomy in the lesson?

choices.text: Bloom → response structure; SOLO → learning type; Gagné → reliability
Bloom → cognitive audit; SOLO → structure of the response; Gagné → kind of learning
Bloom → fairness; SOLO → motivation; Gagné → grading consistency
Bloom → psychometrics; SOLO → criterion validity; Gagné → norm referencing

items.explain: Bloom audits the cognitive operation, SOLO describes the structure of the response, and Gagne describes the kind of learning. Assigning reliability, fairness, motivation, or psychometrics to them invents jobs they do not have.

items.stem: An instructor gives students a short mechanics inventory during the first day of class and changes the opening unit after discovering widespread misconceptions. What role did the assessment serve?

choices.text: Summative
Diagnostic
Norm-referenced
Contractual

items.explain: Diagnostic assessment establishes a starting point so instruction can answer what learners already hold. Summative judges accomplishment, norm referencing compares people, and contractual is not a purpose that fits here.
items.bankWhy: Diagnostic assessment establishes the learner's starting point so instruction can respond to what the learner already knows.

items.stem: An instructor gives the exact same quiz to two sections. In Section A, the results determine final grades. In Section B, the instructor uses the results to reteach misunderstood concepts the next day. What does this illustrate?

choices.text: Formative and summative are properties of how an assessment is used
Multiple-choice assessments are inherently summative
Repeated assessments are inherently formative
The quiz in Section B has greater reliability

items.explain: Formative and summative describe what happens because of the information, not the instrument: section A's quiz settles grades while section B's quiz changes tomorrow's teaching. Format and repetition are not the defining feature.
items.bankWhy: The instrument itself does not determine whether an assessment is formative. What matters is what happens because of the information.

items.stem: According to Black and Wiliam's formulation, which condition is most important for calling an assessment formative?

choices.text: It is worth very few points
Students receive it frequently
Its evidence actually changes what happens next
It contains written comments

items.explain: Black and Wiliam define formative by whether the evidence actually alters what happens next. Few points, high frequency, and written comments are surface features that do not guarantee the evidence gets used.

items.stem: A learning platform gradually replaces essay writing, design work, and discussion with multiple-choice checks because those items can be generated and scored cheaply. Which danger does this most directly illustrate?

choices.text: Stereotype threat
Routine assessment narrowing the course toward what software can grade
Differential item functioning
The standard error of measurement

items.explain: Assessment steers what gets taught, so routine cheap-to-score checks pull a course toward whatever software can grade. Stereotype threat, DIF, and SEM describe entirely different problems.

items.stem: Students either reread a passage several times or retrieve its contents from memory. Immediately afterward, rereaders feel more confident, but one week later the retrieval group remembers more. Which principle does this illustrate?

choices.text: Testing effect
Criteria compliance
Contract grading
Norm referencing

items.explain: Roediger and Karpicke's result is durability: retrieval beats rereading on the delayed test even though rereaders felt more confident. Criteria compliance, contract grading, and norm referencing are unrelated.
items.bankWhy: Roediger and Karpicke's important result concerns durable retention, not merely immediate performance.

items.stem: Why is the **delayed** test in retrieval-practice research especially important?

choices.text: Immediate performance is never measurable
Durable learning can differ from what looks strongest immediately after study
Test reliability increases automatically after seven days
Rereading only works on norm-referenced assessments

items.explain: The delayed test separates durable learning from how strong performance looks immediately after study, which is where the rereading fluency illusion appears. Immediate performance is measurable, reliability does not rise with time, and rereading is not frame-specific.

items.stem: A computerized assessment selects the next problem based on the learner's previous answers and repeatedly chooses items expected to reveal the most information about that learner's proficiency. What kind of assessment is this?

choices.text: Diagnostic only
Adaptive assessment
Ungrading
Holistic assessment

items.explain: Adaptive assessment selects items dynamically to converge on a learner's estimated level. Diagnostic-only, ungrading, and holistic scoring describe different stances rather than dynamic item selection.
items.bankWhy: Adaptive assessments select items dynamically to converge on a learner's estimated level.

items.stem: Which framework provides the psychometric foundation commonly associated with adaptive assessment?

choices.text: Item response theory
SOLO taxonomy
Campbell's Law
Contract grading

items.explain: Item response theory supplies the item-parameter model adaptive delivery depends on. SOLO, Campbell's Law, and contract grading are not psychometric foundations for selecting items.

items.stem: A game infers a learner's understanding of Newtonian mechanics from the way the learner constructs and modifies vehicles, without interrupting play with conventional quizzes. Which assessment style best describes this?

choices.text: Summative assessment
Stealth assessment
Norm-referenced assessment
Specifications grading

items.explain: Stealth assessment infers competency from ongoing play without interrupting it with conventional quizzes. Summative, norm-referenced, and specifications grading are different designs.

items.stem: A simulation team begins its assessment design by listing every mouse movement and button click the software can record. According to evidence-centered design, what is wrong with this approach?

choices.text: The team should start by identifying the competencies it wants to measure
Mouse movements are never valid evidence
Evidence-centered design permits only written assessments
Tasks should be designed before constructs are defined

items.explain: Evidence-centered design runs competency model, then evidence model, then task model, so starting from whatever telemetry exists reverses the logic. Mouse movements can be valid evidence, written-only tasks are not required, and tasks follow constructs.
items.bankWhy: Evidence-centered design proceeds conceptually from **competency model → evidence model → task model**. Starting from cheap telemetry reverses the logic.

items.stem: According to the lesson, which four jobs are simultaneously assigned to grades?

choices.text: Communicate, sort, motivate, give feedback
Measure, punish, remediate, certify
Predict, rank, diagnose, archive
Compare, teach, operationalize, validate

items.explain: Grades are asked to communicate, sort, motivate, and give feedback at the same time. The other lists drop the motivational and feedback jobs or replace them with punishment and certification.

items.stem: Starch and Elliott's early grading studies are most useful for illustrating which problem?

choices.text: Students dislike numerical grades
Different graders can assign dramatically different scores to the same work
Automated grading always outperforms human grading
Norm-referenced exams are inherently unfair

items.explain: Starch and Elliott showed that different graders can assign dramatically different scores to the same work, which is a reliability problem. Student preference, automated superiority, and inherent unfairness are different claims.

items.stem: Why did Douglas Reeves object to averaging a zero into a course grade?

choices.text: Zeros make grading too criterion-referenced
A zero can have a disproportionately destructive arithmetic effect on the average
Students cannot interpret percentages
Zeros increase Cronbach's alpha

items.explain: Reeves objected to the arithmetic damage a zero does inside an average, which is far larger than the missing work deserves. Criterion referencing, percentage interpretation, and alpha are not the objection.

items.stem: One group receives written comments on its work. Another receives only grades. A third receives grades plus comments. In Butler's study, which approach produced the strongest later performance?

choices.text: Grades only
Grades plus comments
Comments only
All three were equivalent

items.explain: Butler found comments alone produced the strongest later performance, because the grade can crowd out attention to feedback. Grades only, grades plus comments, and equivalence were not the outcome.
items.bankWhy: The lesson's larger point is that the grade itself can crowd out attention to feedback.

items.stem: A school stops averaging every task into one percentage and instead reports a student's demonstrated level on each learning standard. Which philosophy most closely fits?

choices.text: Standards-based grading
Contract grading
Ungrading
Norm referencing

items.explain: Standards-based grading reports demonstrated level on each learning standard instead of averaging everything into one percentage. Contract, ungrading, and norm referencing are different philosophies.

items.stem: A course marks each assignment simply **meets specification / does not meet specification**, and students earn course grades by completing defined bundles of satisfactory work. Which approach is this?

choices.text: Standards-based grading
Specifications grading
Contract grading
Ungrading

items.explain: Specifications grading marks each assignment meets or does not meet the specification and awards course grades for bundles of satisfactory work. Standards-based reports per-standard levels, contract changes the basis and control of the grade, and ungrading minimizes grades.

items.stem: Which feature most clearly distinguishes contract grading from standards-based and specifications grading?

choices.text: It always uses a four-point rubric
It changes who determines the basis of the grade and may base it on agreed labor or engagement rather than quality judgments
It forbids revision
It requires students to rank one another

items.explain: Contract grading changes who determines the basis of the grade, often granting credit for agreed labor or engagement rather than a quality judgment. Rubric shape, banned revision, and student ranking are not the distinguishing feature.

items.stem: A design instructor notices students choosing safe work because they are optimizing for marks, and students routinely ignore written critiques after seeing their scores. If the instructor believes the **presence of the grade itself** is causing the problem, which philosophy most directly responds?

choices.text: Ungrading
Norm-referenced grading
Point-based grading
Differential grading

items.explain: If the presence of the grade itself is the diagnosed cause, minimizing or removing the grade is the direct response, which is ungrading. Norm-referenced, point-based, and differential grading all keep the grade central.

items.stem: Which description best captures the lesson's definition of feedback?

choices.text: Any information a teacher gives after grading
Usable information about the gap between current performance and a desired destination
A numerical estimate of ability
Praise intended to motivate the learner

items.explain: Feedback is usable information about the gap between current performance and a desired destination. Information after grading, a numeric ability estimate, and motivational praise all miss the gap plus use requirement.

items.stem: What surprising result emerged from Kluger and DeNisi's meta-analysis?

choices.text: Feedback almost never changed performance
Feedback improved every learner studied
Feedback improved performance on average but made performance worse in a substantial minority of cases
Written feedback consistently outperformed spoken feedback

items.explain: Kluger and DeNisi found feedback improved performance on average while making it worse in a substantial minority of cases. Feedback does change performance, it does not help everyone, and the modality claim is not the finding.
items.bankWhy: Feedback is not automatically beneficial merely because it exists.

items.stem: According to Hattie and Timperley, which example provides the least task-relevant information?

choices.text: “Your evidence does not support the second claim.”
“Try comparing these two cases before drawing your conclusion.”
“Check your reasoning before submitting your next answer.”
“You're a really smart student.”

items.explain: Self-level praise about the person carries the least task information. The other options sit at task, process, or self-regulation level and point attention back at the work.
items.bankWhy: Self-level praise directs attention toward the person or ego and provides little information about how to improve the work.

items.stem: According to Sadler, which sequence is necessary for a learner to use feedback effectively?

choices.text: Receive a grade → compare with peers → repeat the task
Know the standard → compare present performance with it → take action to close the gap
Read a rubric → memorize criteria → request another grade
Receive praise → increase motivation → achieve mastery

items.explain: Sadler's sequence is know the standard, compare present performance against it, then act to close the gap. Grade-and-compare, memorize-rubric, and praise paths skip the learner's own comparison and action.

items.stem: An expert writing instructor immediately knows that an essay “doesn't quite work,” but struggles to fully articulate the accumulated standards underlying that judgment. What term did Sadler use for this kind of expertise?

choices.text: Criterion validity
Guild knowledge
Metacognitive monitoring
Criteria compliance

items.explain: Sadler called this tacit, accumulated expertise guild knowledge. Criterion validity, metacognitive monitoring, and criteria compliance name different constructs.

items.stem: Why can detailed instructor comments fail even when they are accurate?

choices.text: Learners may not share the instructor's underlying conception of what good work looks like
Accurate feedback reduces reliability
Students can only process numerical information
Feedback works only when anonymous

items.explain: Accurate comments still fail when the learner does not share the instructor's conception of what good work looks like. Feedback does not reduce reliability, learners are not limited to numbers, and anonymity is not the issue.

items.stem: A learner receives a comment saying “develop the analysis more deeply” but has no idea what “deep analysis” looks like. Which problem is most directly illustrated?

choices.text: Standard error
Lack of shared guild knowledge
Adaptive testing
Summative interference

items.explain: Without a shared sense of what deep analysis looks like, the comment cannot guide action, which is the guild knowledge gap. Standard error, adaptive testing, and summative interference are unrelated to the failure.

items.stem: What makes **dialogic feedback** different from a conventional feedback message?

choices.text: It is always delivered digitally
Meaning is negotiated through a two-way interaction
It never includes criticism
It eliminates standards

items.explain: Dialogic feedback negotiates meaning through two-way interaction rather than one-way delivery. It can be spoken or written, it may include criticism, and it does not remove standards.

items.stem: Boud and Molloy's “new paradigm” changes feedback primarily by treating it as:

choices.text: A product instructors deliver efficiently
A process learners actively participate in and drive
A score attached to performance
An automated response generated after every answer

items.explain: Boud and Molloy's new paradigm treats feedback as a process learners actively participate in and drive. Efficient delivery, score attachment, and automatic responses keep feedback as something done to the learner.

items.stem: Which student most clearly demonstrates **feedback literacy**?

choices.text: A student who collects every comment but never revises
A student who can interpret the feedback, judge quality, manage an emotional reaction, and take useful action
A student who receives feedback instantly
A student who earns the highest grade without reading comments

items.explain: Feedback literacy is the capacity to interpret comments, judge quality, manage the emotional response, and take useful action. Collecting without revising, instant delivery, and high grades without reading comments show its absence.

items.stem: What sequence best represents constructive alignment?

choices.text: Choose grading software → write assessment → infer objectives
Define outcomes → design learning activities → design assessment around the same target
Write rubric → determine grade distribution → choose objectives
Rank students → identify misconceptions → revise standards

items.explain: Constructive alignment defines outcomes, designs learning activities, then designs assessment around the same target. Software-first, rubric-first, and ranking-first sequences all invert the order.

items.stem: Why does the lesson call reliability a rubric's first job?

choices.text: Rubrics ensure every learner receives the same grade
Rubrics help different graders converge toward similar judgments
Rubrics prove that the intended construct is being measured
Rubrics make every assignment easier

items.explain: A rubric's first job is helping different graders converge on similar judgments. Equal grades, proof of the intended construct, and easier assignments are not what rubrics guarantee.

items.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes analytic and holistic rubrics?

choices.text: Analytic rubrics judge the whole performance; holistic rubrics score dimensions separately
Analytic rubrics score criteria separately; holistic rubrics make an overall judgment
Analytic rubrics are for novices only
Holistic rubrics cannot be reliable

items.explain: Analytic rubrics score criteria separately while holistic rubrics make one overall judgment. The first option reverses them, and neither design is reserved for novices or inherently unreliable.

items.stem: A history assessment originally asks, “Identify the important causes of World War I.” The published rubric then says, “2 points each for correctly describing the **three** major causes.” Why might this change what the assessment measures?

choices.text: Students are now told how many causes they need to recognize
The rubric reduces inter-rater reliability
Students must now use higher-order cognition
Three causes cannot be assessed analytically

items.explain: Telling students there are exactly three acceptable causes gives away how many exist, so recognizing the scope stops being part of what is measured. It does not lower inter-rater reliability, demand higher-order cognition, or block analytic scoring.
items.bankWhy: The rubric has leaked information about the expected scope of the answer. Recognizing how many important causes exist is no longer part of the construct.

items.stem: Students begin writing essays by mechanically checking off every phrase in a detailed rubric rather than making substantive judgments about the topic. Which concept best describes the problem?

choices.text: Criteria compliance
Stereotype threat
Retrieval practice
Differential item functioning

items.explain: Checking off rubric phrases instead of judging the topic is criteria compliance. Stereotype threat, retrieval practice, and DIF describe different phenomena.

items.stem: A professor argues that because transparency is good, students at every level should receive the most detailed possible grading rubric before every task. Which response best matches the lesson?

choices.text: Correct: maximum transparency can never affect validity
Incorrect: the appropriate level of rubric detail depends on what judgment the assessment is intended to measure
Correct, but only for norm-referenced assessments
Incorrect because students should never see rubrics

items.explain: How much rubric detail is appropriate depends on the judgment the assessment is meant to measure, because an overly detailed rubric can hand over the thinking being assessed. Transparency is not weightless, is not limited to norm-referenced tests, and does not mean hiding rubrics.
items.bankWhy: If independent judgment is itself part of the target construct, an overly detailed rubric can give away the very thinking being assessed.

items.stem: According to Jonsson and Svingby's review, when are rubrics especially effective at improving scoring reliability?

choices.text: When students never see examples
When rubrics are accompanied by exemplars and grader training
When every criterion is worth exactly the same points
When holistic scoring is prohibited

items.explain: Jonsson and Svingby found rubrics help scoring reliability most when paired with exemplars and grader training. Withholding examples, equal weighting, and banning holistic scoring are not their findings.

items.stem: Why does peer assessment have educational value even if an instructor could grade every submission personally?

choices.text: Reviewing another person's work can itself produce learning
Peer grades are always more accurate than expert grades
Students prefer giving grades to receiving feedback
Peer assessment eliminates bias

items.explain: Reviewing someone else's work is itself a learning activity, so peer assessment has value even when the instructor could grade everything personally. Peer marks are not automatically more accurate, and preference or bias elimination is not the reason.

items.stem: What did Falchikov and Goldfinch's pooled evidence suggest about peer marks?

choices.text: Peer and teacher marks bear almost no relationship
Peer marks correlate reasonably well with teacher marks on average
Peer marks are always identical to teacher marks
Peer marks work only in graduate courses

items.explain: Falchikov and Goldfinch's pooled evidence found peer and teacher marks correlate reasonably well on average. Near-zero relation, perfect agreement, and graduate-course-only limits are not what the evidence showed.

items.stem: Which peer-review design tends to correspond better with expert judgment according to the lesson?

choices.text: Students score dozens of tiny checklist dimensions independently
Students make a more holistic judgment against well-understood criteria
Students grade without seeing any criteria
Students assign scores randomly and average them

items.explain: Peer designs where students make a more holistic judgment against well-understood criteria tend to correspond better with expert judgment. Dozens of tiny checklist dimensions, unstated criteria, and random averaging all degrade agreement.

items.stem: A course increases from two peer graders per assignment to eight, yet a systematic tendency to penalize unconventional writing styles remains. Why has averaging failed?

choices.text: Averaging only helps when errors are independent and random
Eight raters are fewer than the minimum required
Reliability always decreases as raters are added
Peer graders cannot produce quantitative scores

items.explain: Averaging cancels independent random error, not bias shared by every rater, so adding graders reproduces the same penalty. Eight raters is not below a minimum, reliability does not always fall as raters are added, and peers can produce quantitative marks.
items.bankWhy: Shared bias does not cancel out merely because more people reproduce it.

items.stem: What distinguishes **fairness** from **reliability** in peer assessment?

choices.text: Reliability asks whether marks are consistent; fairness asks whether systematic consistency comes from irrelevant features rather than the work itself
Reliability concerns students, fairness concerns teachers
Fairness is simply another word for high inter-rater reliability
Reliability matters only with numerical grading

items.explain: Reliability asks whether marks are consistent while fairness asks whether that consistency comes from irrelevant features rather than the work itself. The other options misassign the terms, equate them, or restrict reliability to numbers.

items.stem: A large MOOC already has students review one another's work. Expert graders later grade the assignment but currently ignore those peer reviews. Which redesign follows the meta-reviewer model?

choices.text: Replace experts entirely with peers
Let expert graders evaluate the work while seeing the peer reviews it already received
Average all peer grades and automatically accept the result
Have experts review only students who complain

items.explain: The meta-review model has expert graders judge the work with the peer reviews it already received in view. Replacing experts, auto-accepting averaged peer marks, and reviewing only complaints drop expert judgment or the review signal.
items.bankWhy: The meta-review model composes peer and expert review rather than treating them as mutually exclusive.

items.stem: Which three principles form the core of the Belmont Report?

choices.text: Validity, reliability, fairness
Respect for persons, beneficence, justice
Privacy, anonymity, transparency
Consent, prediction, optimization

items.explain: The Belmont Report rests on respect for persons, beneficence, and justice. Validity, reliability, and fairness are measurement ideas, privacy and anonymity name practices, and consent, prediction, and optimization is not the trio.

items.stem: What is the primary role of an Institutional Review Board in human-subjects research?

choices.text: Publish the study after completion
Approve and review research protections before the research begins
Determine whether results are statistically significant
Grade research participants fairly

items.explain: An IRB approves and reviews research protections before the research begins. Publishing results, testing statistical significance, and grading participants are not its role.

items.stem: A professor tells students that participating in her study is “completely optional,” but she is also the person assigning their course grades. Several students participate because they do not want to disappoint her. Which ethical concept is most directly implicated?

choices.text: Explicit coercion only
Undue influence
Differential item functioning
Criterion validity

items.explain: The quiet pressure of not wanting to disappoint the person who grades you is undue influence. Coercion names explicit threats, while DIF and criterion validity belong to measurement rather than research ethics.
items.bankWhy: The pressure need not be an explicit threat. The power relationship itself can make supposedly voluntary participation less voluntary.

items.stem: Why are students sometimes described as a **captive population** in educational research?

choices.text: They are legally forbidden from leaving a study
They occupy an institutional relationship in which instructors control grades, opportunities, and classroom conditions
Educational studies must always involve minors
Students cannot provide informed consent

items.explain: Students are described as captive because instructors control grades, opportunities, and classroom conditions, which makes refusal costly. They are not legally bound, minors are not required, and they can provide informed consent.

items.stem: Which law most directly governs access to students' education records such as grades and transcripts?

choices.text: FERPA
HIPAA
Campbell's Law
The Belmont Report

items.explain: FERPA governs access to students' education records such as grades and transcripts. HIPAA covers health information, Campbell's Law is about indicators under stakes, and the Belmont Report is a principles framework.

items.stem: A student agrees in 2024 to let researchers use interaction data to study a tutoring system. In 2030, another research group wants to reuse those records to predict which students will drop out. What does the Week 5 stewardship principle suggest?

choices.text: The original consent automatically licenses any future research
The new purpose should be reconsidered rather than assuming the old consent covers it
Data may never be reused under any circumstance
Reuse is automatically acceptable if computation is performed by an algorithm

items.explain: A new purpose should be reconsidered rather than assumed covered by an old consent. Blanket reuse, a total ban on reuse, and automatic algorithm exemption are all wrong.

items.stem: Why is **inBloom** used as a cautionary example?

choices.text: It showed that centralized educational data can trigger serious public and parental privacy concerns
It proved adaptive testing cannot work
It eliminated student records too quickly
It showed that rubrics reduce validity

items.explain: inBloom is cautionary because centralized educational data triggered serious public and parental privacy concerns. It was not about adaptive testing failing, deleting records too quickly, or rubric validity.

items.stem: What is **equipoise**?

choices.text: The belief that both conditions will produce identical results
Genuine uncertainty about which experimental condition is better
Equality in the number of participants per group
A requirement that students know which group they are in

items.explain: Equipoise is genuine uncertainty about which experimental condition is better, which is what can make random assignment acceptable. Identical results, equal group sizes, and disclosure requirements are different ideas.

items.stem: A school believes with near certainty that a new intervention is substantially better for students but deliberately assigns half its students to what administrators already believe is the inferior option simply to obtain a publishable comparison. Which concept creates the strongest ethical concern?

choices.text: Criterion validity
Equipoise
Internal consistency
Evidence-centered design

items.explain: If administrators are nearly certain one arm is better, randomizing students into the other arm for publishability violates equipoise. Criterion validity, internal consistency, and evidence-centered design do not address the ethics.

items.stem: What lesson does the Facebook emotional-contagion study illustrate in the Week 5 material?

choices.text: Any software optimization is automatically exempt from research ethics
Optimization combined with an intention to produce generalizable research can cross into research that carries research obligations
Online experiments can never produce valid evidence
A/B tests are unethical while untested product changes are always ethical

items.explain: Optimization plus an intention to produce generalizable knowledge can cross into research that carries research obligations. Software does not exempt ethics, online experiments can yield valid evidence, and A/B tests are not inherently unethical.

items.stem: Which research practice most closely matches the lesson's idea of responsible stewardship?

choices.text: Collect every possible variable in case it becomes useful later
Assume researcher neutrality unless evidence proves otherwise
Minimize unnecessary data, respect participants, and remain skeptical of one's own neutrality
Keep data indefinitely because storage is inexpensive

items.explain: Responsible stewardship means collecting only what is needed, respecting participants, and staying skeptical of one's own neutrality. Collecting everything, assuming neutrality, and indefinite storage are the failure modes.

items.stem: A school makes one standardized test score the primary basis for graduation, teacher evaluation, school rankings, and funding. Schools respond by devoting increasingly large portions of instruction to maximizing that score. Which principle most directly predicts this outcome?

choices.text: Campbell's Law
SOLO taxonomy
Cronbach's alpha
Dialogic feedback

items.explain: The more a quantitative indicator drives high-stakes decisions, the stronger the pressure to optimize the indicator instead of the process, which is Campbell's Law. SOLO, alpha, and dialogic feedback do not predict that response.
items.bankWhy: The more a quantitative indicator becomes the basis of high-stakes decisions, the stronger the pressure to corrupt or optimize the indicator rather than the underlying process.

items.stem: How is Goodhart's Law related to Campbell's Law in this lesson?

choices.text: Both warn that attaching high stakes to a proxy can cause people to optimize the proxy rather than the thing it was intended to represent
Both provide methods for increasing reliability
Both explain stereotype threat
Both argue against educational measurement entirely

items.explain: Both warn that attaching high stakes to a proxy pushes people to optimize the proxy rather than the thing it was meant to represent. Neither is a reliability method, an explanation of stereotype threat, or an argument against measurement.

items.stem: Why does an assessment's fairness obligation become especially important when the system is deployed at large scale?

choices.text: Statistical error vanishes at scale
The same systematic bias can be imposed on a very large population simultaneously
Large systems automatically become norm-referenced
Small assessments cannot be biased

items.explain: At scale the same systematic bias is imposed on a very large population at once, so the fairness obligation grows rather than shrinks. Statistical error does not vanish, large systems are not automatically norm-referenced, and small assessments can be biased.

items.stem: An automated essay scorer is trained on thousands of historical human ratings. The developers argue that because the final judgments are produced by software, the system is more objective than humans. What is the strongest objection from the lesson?

choices.text: Software cannot process written language
A model trained on historical judgments can reproduce those judgments' biases while making them appear objective
Historical datasets are always too small
Automated scoring can only be used formatively

items.explain: A model trained on historical human ratings can reproduce those judgments' biases while wrapping them in apparent objectivity. Software can process language, dataset size is not the issue, and automated scoring is not limited to formative use.

items.stem: Why is Les Perelman's work with elaborate but meaningless machine-generated essays important?

choices.text: It demonstrates the testing effect
It shows automated scoring systems may reward surface features correlated with quality rather than genuine quality
It proves humans cannot evaluate essays reliably
It shows that longer essays are always better

items.explain: Perelman's machine-generated essays show scorers can reward surface features correlated with quality rather than genuine quality. It does not demonstrate the testing effect, prove human unreliability, or show longer essays are better.

items.stem: The 2020 UK exam-grading episode is used primarily to illustrate what danger?

choices.text: Adaptive assessment becomes inefficient at national scale
Algorithmic decisions can reproduce and amplify disadvantage across a population while appearing neutral
Holistic grading cannot be automated
Criterion-referenced grading requires human scorers

items.explain: The 2020 UK episode shows algorithmic decisions reproducing and amplifying disadvantage across a population while appearing neutral. It is not about adaptive inefficiency, automating holistic grading, or requiring human scorers.

items.stem: Which design best matches the lesson's standard for accountable machine judgment?

choices.text: The model's decision is final because automation removes human bias
Decisions should be inspectable, audited, appealable, and ultimately answerable to people
Learners should not be told that algorithms are involved
Human review should be prohibited because it reduces consistency

items.explain: Accountable machine judgment means decisions are inspectable, audited, appealable, and answerable to people. Final-by-default, hidden involvement, and banning human review all remove accountability.

items.stem: A testing platform logs webcam data, mouse trajectories, keystrokes, location information, and device fingerprints “because the analytics team may want them someday,” although none of those data are necessary to score the assessment. Which principle most directly objects?

choices.text: Assessment data stewardship
Bloom's hierarchy
Criterion referencing
Testing effect

items.explain: Stewardship calls for collecting only what the assessment requires, explaining what is captured, securing it, and avoiding unrelated repurposing. Bloom, criterion referencing, and the testing effect are unrelated.
items.bankWhy: The lesson argues for collecting only what the assessment requires, explaining what is captured and why, securing it, and avoiding unrelated repurposing.

items.stem: A product team argues, “We are not conducting publishable research, so no IRB is involved. Therefore we have no ethical obligation to minimize the educational data we collect.” Which response best follows from the lesson?

choices.text: Correct; privacy obligations apply only to formal research
Correct if users accepted terms of service
Incorrect; learners retain privacy interests even when the activity is ordinary assessment rather than formal research
Incorrect only if the assessment is summative

items.explain: Learners keep privacy interests even when the activity is ordinary assessment rather than formal research, so no IRB does not mean no obligation. Formal-research-only, terms of service, and summative-only conditions are all wrong.

items.stem: What does the lesson mean by **humility as a stance** toward assessment scores?

choices.text: Never make decisions using scores
Treat scores as perfectly precise when reliability is high
Use assessment evidence when necessary while remembering that the score is an imperfect proxy rather than the learner itself
Replace every score with peer assessment

items.explain: Humility means using assessment evidence when necessary while remembering the score is an imperfect proxy rather than the learner. Never using scores, trusting high reliability as precision, and replacing scores with peer assessment are the extremes.

items.stem: A course's learning objective says students will **design an original experiment**, but the final exam consists entirely of definitions of experimental terminology. The exam has Cronbach's alpha of .95. Which criticism is strongest?

choices.text: The exam cannot be reliable because it contains vocabulary questions
The assessment is highly consistent but poorly aligned with the intended construct
Original experiments cannot be assessed reliably
Cronbach's alpha demonstrates that the learning objective has been achieved

items.explain: High alpha cannot rescue misalignment: the exam consistently measures terminology recall rather than designing an experiment. Vocabulary items can be reliable, original experiments can be assessed, and alpha says nothing about achieving the objective.
items.bankWhy: High reliability cannot rescue a validity/alignment problem. The assessment consistently measures something other than the intended performance.

items.stem: A professor gives a diagnostic quiz at the start of class, discovers that half the class holds a serious misconception, records the result, and proceeds with the original lesson plan unchanged. What is the strongest criticism?

choices.text: Diagnostic testing should only occur after instruction
The instructor collected diagnostic information but failed to use it to change the instructional path
The quiz has become norm-referenced
The quiz violates Campbell's Law

items.explain: The instructor gathered diagnostic evidence and then changed nothing, so it never became formative. Diagnostic testing belongs before instruction, the quiz is not norm-referenced, and Campbell's Law concerns high-stakes indicators.

items.stem: Students are told exactly which five phrases must appear in an essay to receive full points. Almost every student includes all five, but many essays show little understanding. Which pair of concepts best explains the problem?

choices.text: Criteria compliance and the granularity/transparency trap
Retrieval practice and adaptive testing
Stereotype threat and differential item functioning
Standard error and criterion validity

items.explain: Students checking off five required phrases while understanding little is criteria compliance produced by granular, fully transparent requirements. Retrieval practice, adaptive testing, stereotype threat, DIF, SEM, and criterion validity do not explain it.

items.stem: An online tutor instantly tells students “correct” or “incorrect” after every response but never helps them interpret why an answer failed or what standard distinguishes good reasoning. Which criticism best fits the feedback section?

choices.text: The system provides scalable task-level information but lacks the dialogic process that helps learners construct and use meaning
Automated feedback can never improve learning
Immediate feedback is necessarily summative
The system should replace comments with grades

items.explain: Instant correct or incorrect marks give scalable task-level information but no dialogic process for building shared meaning about why an answer failed. Automated feedback can help learning, immediacy is not inherently summative, and replacing comments with grades loses information.

items.stem: A peer-grading system produces very consistent grades, but students using nonstandard dialects systematically receive lower scores despite equivalent content. What is the best interpretation?

choices.text: High reliability demonstrates fairness
The system may be reliable while still unfair and therefore invalid for the intended judgment
The only problem is low internal consistency
Adding more similarly biased peer graders will necessarily eliminate the difference

items.explain: Consistent marks can still come from dialect rather than content, which makes the system reliable yet unfair and therefore invalid for the intended judgment. Consistency does not prove fairness, internal consistency is not the problem, and adding similarly biased raters preserves the bias.

items.stem: A video game records dozens of player actions. Designers discover afterward that one action correlates with course grades, so they declare that action a valid measure of “systems thinking.” What is missing from the evidence-centered approach?

choices.text: A competency model establishing what systems thinking means before choosing evidence for it
A norm table
A contract-grading agreement
An analytic rubric

items.explain: The competency model has to define what systems thinking means before evidence is chosen for it. A norm table, a contract agreement, and an analytic rubric do not supply that definition.

items.stem: A school introduces an AI writing score worth 70% of students' final grades. Within a semester, students learn that longer sentences and unusual vocabulary increase the automated score, so they begin producing verbose but less coherent essays. Which concept most directly explains the behavioral response?

choices.text: Goodhart/Campbell
Stereotype threat
Retrieval practice
Guild knowledge

items.explain: Once the automated score is the high-stakes target, students optimize the proxy and produce verbose but less coherent essays. Stereotype threat, retrieval practice, and guild knowledge are different ideas.
items.bankWhy: Once the proxy becomes the high-stakes target, people optimize the proxy.

items.stem: A professor says, “My rubric is extremely detailed, so my assessment must be valid.” What is the strongest objection?

choices.text: Rubrics reduce reliability
A detailed rubric can improve scoring consistency while simultaneously changing or narrowing the construct being assessed
Valid assessments cannot use rubrics
Holistic rubrics are always more valid

items.explain: A detailed rubric can improve scoring consistency while simultaneously narrowing or changing what is assessed, so detail is not proof of validity. Rubrics do not reduce reliability, validity does not forbid rubrics, and holistic is not automatically more valid.
